chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Suleym, the slave of Ali ibn Yaqteen, who said: He used to suffer from conjunctivitis in his eyes.

He said: Abu Al-Hassan (peace be upon him) wrote to him, initiating from himself: 'What is preventing you from using the kohl of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)? It is one part of Rabahiyya camphor and one part of Asqutry aloe. They are crushed together and sifted with silk. You should apply it like the application of antimony, one application in the month. It drives away every illness in the head and expels it from the body.' He said: So he used to apply it, and he did not complain about his eyes until he died.

key_terms.أَصْقُوطْرَى: Asqutry (a type of aloe or medicinal plant)

ai.seo_question: What is the prescribed treatment for eye diseases in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the Shia tradition of *al-Tibb al-Nabawi* (Prophetic Medicine) by presenting Imam Al-Hassan (as) as a source of specialized medical knowledge, specifically prescribing a compound of camphor and aloe for Suleym ibn Yaqteen. The text emphasizes the therapeutic efficacy of this kohl not only for local eye ailments but also for systemic head conditions, reflecting the holistic view of health in Imami scholarship. The narrative serves as both a practical medical guide and a testament to the Imam's authority in curing physical afflictions through divine wisdom.
